Marked length spectrum rigidity
for Anosov magnetic surfaces

Valerio Assenza and Jacopo de Simoi,
James Marshall Reber and Ivo Terek Address: Instituto de Matemática Pura e Aplicada, Rio de Janeiro, RJ, 22460-320, Brazil Email address: valerio.assenza@impa.br Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada Email address: jacopods@math.utoronto.ca Address: Department of Mathematics, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, 43210, USA Email address: marshallreber.1@osu.edu Address: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, Williams College, Williamstown, MA, 01267, USA Email address: it3@williams.edu
Abstract.

We show that if MM is a closed, connected, oriented surface, and two Anosov magnetic systems on MM are conjugate by a volume-preserving conjugacy isotopic to the identity, with their magnetic forms in the same cohomology class, then the metrics are isometric. This extends the recent result by Guillarmou, Lefeuvre, and Paternain to the magnetic setting.

1. Introduction

Let MM be a closed, connected, oriented manifold, and let gg be a Riemannian metric on MM. Denoting the corresponding geodesic flow on its unit tangent bundle by φgt:Sg​M→Sg​M\varphi_{g}^{t}:S_{g}M\rightarrow S_{g}M and denoting the infinitesimal generator of the flow by XgX^{g}, we say that the metric gg is Anosov if φgt\varphi_{g}^{t} is an Anosov flow, i.e., there exists a φgt\varphi_{g}^{t}-invariant splitting T​Sg​M=E+⊕ℝ​Xg⊕E−TS_{g}M=E^{+}\oplus\mathds{R}X^{g}\oplus E^{-} and constants c,d>0c,d>0 so that for all t≥0t\geq 0 and ξ∈E±​(v)\xi\in E^{\pm}(v), we have

(1.1) ‖dv​φg∓t​(ξ)‖≤d​e−c​t​‖ξ‖,\|d_{v}\varphi_{g}^{\mp t}(\xi)\|\leq de^{-ct}\|\xi\|,

where ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| denotes the norm coming from the Sasaki metric on Sg​MS_{g}M.

Anosov metrics can be seen as a generalization of negatively curved metrics [1] and, as such, they share many common qualities. For example, observe that if gg is an Anosov metric, then for every non-trivial free homotopy class ν∈π1​(M)\nu\in\pi_{1}(M), there is a unique closed gg-geodesic γν∈ν\gamma_{\nu}\in\nu [31]. The marked length spectrum is defined to be the function MLS⁡(g):π1​(M)→[0,∞){{\rm MLS}(g):\pi_{1}(M)\rightarrow[0,\infty)} which assigns to a non-trivial free homotopy class ν\nu the length of its geodesic representative γν\gamma_{\nu}, and 00 to the trivial free homotopy class. It is conjectured that MLS⁡(g){\rm MLS}(g) uniquely characterizes the Anosov metric gg. More precisely:

Conjecture 1.1 ([28]).

Let g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} be two Anosov metrics on MM. If MLS⁡(g1)=MLS⁡(g2){\rm MLS}(g_{1})={\rm MLS}(g_{2}), then g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} are isometric by an isometry which is isotopic to the identity.

In the case where g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} are both negatively curved metrics, this is the well-known Burns-Katok conjecture [10]. Using Livshits’ theorem [32] along with an argument by Gromov [26], one can show that if MLS⁡(g1)=MLS⁡(g2){\rm MLS}(g_{1})={\rm MLS}(g_{2}), then there is a C0C^{0}-conjugacy between the corresponding geodesic flows which is isotopic to the identity. With this in mind, the conjecture broadly states that dynamical invariants give rise to geometric rigidity. It is known that Conjecture  1.1 holds for non-positively curved metrics on surfaces [14, 16, 38], and for negatively curved metrics in dimensions three and higher when one of the metrics is locally symmetric [8, 29]. For Anosov metrics, the conjecture has been recently proved for surfaces in [28]; a local version (i.e. when the metrics are sufficiently close in an appropriate topology) holds in arbitrary dimension, provided the metrics have non-positive sectional curvature [27]. The conjecture is still open in general.

In this paper, we bring the above discussion to the context of magnetic dynamics. Namely, we study marked length spectrum rigidity for Riemannian metrics on surfaces in presence of a magnetic field. Magnetic dynamics was formalized in [2, 3], and has been investigated in many works in the last decades. For a general overview, we refer the reader to [5], and the references therein.

From now on, let MM be a closed, connected, orientable surface. A magnetic system is a pair (g,b)(g,b), with gg a Riemannian metric on MM and bb a smooth function (referred to as the magnetic intensity) on MM. Denote by Ωg\Omega_{g} the area form induced by gg on MM, and let ii be the complex structure given by the orientation of Ωg\Omega_{g}. More precisely, given a vector v∈T​Mv\in TM, i​viv is the rotation of vv by the angle π/2\pi/2 according to the orientation. A curve γ:ℝ→M\gamma:\mathds{R}\to M is a (g,b)(g,b)-geodesic if it satisfies the differential equation

(1.2) D​γ˙d​t​(t)=b⁡(γ⁡(t))​i​γ˙​(t),\frac{\mathrm{D}\dot{\gamma}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)=b(\gamma(t))i\dot{\gamma}(t),

where D/d​t{\rm D}/{\rm d}t denotes the covariant derivative along γ\gamma induced by the Levi-Civita connection of gg. A (g,b)(g,b)-geodesic describes the motion of a charged particle on (M,g)(M,g) under the influence of a magnetic force described by bb.

Observe that if b=0b=0, then (1.2) reduces to the standard equation for gg-geodesics on MM. Also observe that while (g,b)(g,b)-geodesics have constant speed, they are not homogeneous if b≠0b\neq 0. In particular, rescaling the initial speed vector or inverting the direction of the initial velocity vector may drastically change the associated trajectory. Despite this, up to a time reparameterization, one can recover the dynamics of unit speed (g,b)(g,b)-geodesics from the dynamics of (g,b)(g,b)-geodesics with speed s>0s>0 by rescaling the metric gg by the factor 1/s21/s^{2} and the magnetic intensity by the factor 1/s1/s. Without loss of generality, we restrict our perspective to unit speed solutions of (1.2).

The magnetic flow associated to the pair (g,b)(g,b) is the flow φg,bt:Sg​M→Sg​M\varphi_{g,b}^{t}:S_{g}M\rightarrow S_{g}M given by φg,bt​(γ⁡(0),γ˙​(0))≔(γ⁡(t),γ˙​(t))\varphi_{g,b}^{t}(\gamma(0),\dot{\gamma}(0))\coloneqq(\gamma(t),\dot{\gamma}(t)). The orbits of φg,bt\varphi_{g,b}^{t} have a geometric interpretation in terms of the geodesic curvature. The gg-geodesic curvature associated to a curve γ:ℝ→M\gamma:\mathds{R}\rightarrow M is defined by

kg​(t)≔g⁡(D​γ˙d​t​(t),i​γ˙​(t)).\mathrm{k}^{g}(t)\coloneqq g\left(\frac{\mathrm{D}\dot{\gamma}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t),i\dot{\gamma}(t)\right).

It is immediate from (1.2) that a unit speed curve γ\gamma is a (g,b)(g,b)-geodesic if and only if the gg-geodesic curvature of γ\gamma satisfies kg​(t)=b⁡(γ⁡(t))\mathrm{k}^{g}(t)=b(\gamma(t)).

The magnetic system (g,b)(g,b) is called an Anosov magnetic system if the flow φg,bt\varphi_{g,b}^{t} is Anosov. Similar to the geodesic scenario, the existence of an Anosov magnetic system on MM implies some restrictions on both the magnetic intensity and the surface. By [35, Corollary C], the genus of MM must be at least two and, as pointed out in [11, Theorem B], the average of the magnetic intensity cannot be larger than the so-called Mañé critical value.

An interesting problem is determining how to construct Anosov magnetic systems. By the structural stability of Anosov flows, observe that if gg is an Anosov metric, then (g,b)(g,b) is Anosov as long as bb is uniformly small. On the other hand, not every Anosov magnetic system comes from an Anosov metric: in [11, Section 7], it was shown that one can start with a non-Anosov metric on a higher genus surface and place a magnetic intensity bb on MM so that (g,b)(g,b) is Anosov. This shows that the set of metrics for which there is a magnetic intensity bb so that (g,b)(g,b) is Anosov is larger than the set of Anosov metrics.

As in the Riemannian setting, an important subset of the set of Anosov magnetic systems consists of those which are negatively curved in a magnetic sense. The magnetic curvature associated to the system (g,b)(g,b) is given by

(1.3) 𝕂g,b:Sg​M→ℝ𝕂g,b​(x,v)≔Kg​(x)−dx​b​(i​v)+b2​(x),\mathbb{K}^{g,b}:S_{g}M\rightarrow\mathds{R}\quad\mathbb{K}^{g,b}(x,v)\coloneqq K^{g}(x)-\mathrm{d}_{x}b(iv)+b^{2}(x),

where KgK^{g} is the Gaussian curvature of (M,g)(M,g). It was shown in [42] that if 𝕂g,b<0\mathbb{K}^{g,b}<0, then the magnetic flow is Anosov.11 1 See also [24, 25] for earlier works in this direction, and [5, Appendix A] for the proof in higher dimensions. Under additional assumptions, this result has been extended to non-positively curved magnetic flows in the recent paper [35] of the third author in collaboration with Yumin Shen.

Given an Anosov magnetic system (g,b)(g,b), it is still true that for each non-trivial free homotopy class, there is a unique closed (g,b)(g,b)-geodesic with unit speed [13]. With this in mind, we define the magnetic marked length spectrum as the function MLS(g,b):π1(M)→[0,+∞)\mathrm{MLS}(g,b):\pi_{1}(M)\to[0,+\infty) which associates to a non-trivial free homotopy class ν\nu the length of the unique closed unit speed (g,b)(g,b)-geodesic γν\gamma_{\nu} in ν\nu, and zero to the trivial free homotopy class.

Remark 1.2.

Observe that in the Riemannian case, the traces of γν\gamma_{\nu} and γ−ν\gamma_{-\nu} always coincide. This is not necessarily the case for magnetic geodesics. In particular, for some ν\nu, it may be that MLS⁡(g,b)​(ν)≠MLS⁡(g,b)​(−ν)\mathrm{MLS}(g,b)(\nu)\neq\mathrm{MLS}(g,b)(-\nu), although there are non-trivial examples where there is equality for every choice of ν\nu (e.g. Lemma 4.1).

Our main result shows that the magnetic marked length spectrum, the area, and the cohomology class of [b​Ωg][b\Omega_{g}] determine the Riemannian metric and the magnetic intensity, extending the result of the third author in [34] from the deformative setting to the global setting.

Theorem 1.3.

Let MM be a closed, connected, oriented surface. Suppose (g1,b1)(g_{1},b_{1}) and (g2,b2)(g_{2},b_{2}) are Anosov magnetic systems on MM satisfying the following conditions:

MLS⁡(g1,b1)=MLS⁡(g2,b2),Area⁡(g1)=Area⁡(g2),and​[b1​Ωg1]=[b2​Ωg2].{\rm MLS}(g_{1},b_{1})={\rm MLS}(g_{2},b_{2}),\ {\rm Area}(g_{1})={\rm Area}(g_{2}),\ \mbox{and}\ [b_{1}\Omega_{g_{1}}]=[b_{2}\Omega_{g_{2}}].

Then there exists a diffeomorphism f:M→Mf:M\rightarrow M which is isotopic to the identity and which satisfies f∗​(g2)=g1f^{*}(g_{2})=g_{1} and f∗​(b2)=b1f^{*}(b_{2})=b_{1}.

It follows from Livshits’ theorem [32] along with a theorem of Ghys [21] that equality of the marked length spectrum implies that there is a C0C^{0}-conjugacy between the corresponding magnetic flows which is isotopic to the identity. In the case where the magnetic intensities are trivial, one can use the work of Feldman-Ornstein [20] to deduce that the conjugacy is smooth. The recent rigidity result by Gogolev-Rodriguez Hertz in [23, Theorem 1.1] extends this work to a larger class of Anosov flows on three manifolds, and, in particular, shows that equality of the magnetic marked length spectrum implies that the flows φg1,b1t\varphi_{g_{1},b_{1}}^{t} and φg2,b2t\varphi_{g_{2},b_{2}}^{t} are C∞C^{\infty}-conjugate by some h:Sg1​M→Sg2​Mh:S_{g_{1}}M\rightarrow S_{g_{2}}M which is isotopic to the identity (cf. [41]).

Let αg\alpha^{g} be the contact form associated to the geodesic flow φgt\varphi_{g}^{t}. Recall that the Liouville volume form on Sg​MS_{g}M associated to the metric gg is the top-degree form μg≔−αg∧d​αg\mu^{g}\coloneqq-\alpha^{g}\wedge{\mathrm{d}}\alpha^{g}. As we will see in Lemma  2.1, one can use the area assumption to show that the conjugacy described above must pullback the Liouville volume form for g2g_{2} to the Liouville volume form of g1g_{1}, and thus we can reduce Theorem  1.3 to the following.

Theorem 1.4.

Let MM be a closed, connected, oriented surface. Suppose (g1,b1)(g_{1},b_{1}) and (g2,b2)(g_{2},b_{2}) are Anosov magnetic systems on MM such that the corresponding magnetic flows are smoothly conjugate by a conjugacy hh which is isotopic to the identity, the conjugacy hh preserves the corresponding Liouville volume forms, and [b1​Ωg1]=[b2​Ωg2][b_{1}\Omega_{g_{1}}]=[b_{2}\Omega_{g_{2}}]. Then there is a diffeomorphism f:M→Mf:M\rightarrow M which is isotopic to the identity and which satisfies f∗​(g2)=g1f^{*}(g_{2})=g_{1} and f∗​(b2)=b1f^{*}(b_{2})=b_{1}.

The proof of Theorem  1.4 is as follows. First, we use a recent rigidity result by Echevarría Cuesta in [18, Theorem 1.1] to reduce the problem to the setting where g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} are conformally related. Once in this setting, we adapt the conformal argument of Katok in [30] in the magnetic setting. In the case where [b1​Ωg1]=[b2​Ωg2]=0[b_{1}\Omega_{g_{1}}]=[b_{2}\Omega_{g_{2}}]=0, the argument follows by using the fact that magnetic geodesics are minimizers for a functional which we call the magnetic length. In the non-exact setting, we use the fact that the flow is homologically full to work on homologically trivial orbits, and then take advantage of the fact that b1​Ωg1b_{1}\Omega_{g_{1}} and b2​Ωg2b_{2}\Omega_{g_{2}} are exact when pulled back to the unit tangent bundle.

We note that the assumptions on the area and the cohomology class in Theorem  1.3 are necessary via two examples in Section  4, which can also be found in [39]. For the area assumption, we show in Lemma  4.1 that for a hyperbolic metric gg and a constant |b|<1|b|<1, we have MLS(g,b)=(1−b2)−1/2MLS(g){\rm MLS}(g,b)=(1-b^{2})^{-1/2}{\rm MLS}(g). By considering the homothetic metric gb≔(1−b2)−1g_{b}\coloneqq(1-b^{2})^{-1}, we see that MLS⁡(g,b)=MLS⁡(gb){\rm MLS}(g,b)={\rm MLS}(g_{b}) while Area​(g)≠Area​(gb)\text{Area}(g)\neq\text{Area}(g_{b}). It follows that the marked length spectrum assumption alone is not enough to guarantee that the underlying metrics are isometric.

We show in Lemma  2.2 that [b1​Ωg1]=±[b2​Ωg2][b_{1}\Omega_{g_{1}}]=\pm[b_{2}\Omega_{g_{2}}] (see also [39, Lemma 4.1] and [18, Proposition 4.5]). Lemma  4.2 shows that this is actually realizable, in the sense that for a hyperbolic metric gg and a constant |b|<1|b|<1, the magnetic systems (g,b)(g,b) and (g,−b)(g,-b) are smoothly conjugate by a conjugacy which is isotopic to the identity. In particular, this shows that the marked length spectrum assumption alone is not sufficient to guarantee that the cohomology class of b1​Ωg1b_{1}\Omega_{g_{1}} and b2​Ωg2b_{2}\Omega_{g_{2}} are the same.

We now give some applications of Theorem  1.3. First, we observe that Theorem  1.3 extends [27, Theorem 1.1] to the case of exact magnetic systems, i.e., magnetic systems where [b​Ωg]=0[b\Omega_{g}]=0. Using Lemma 2.2, it can be shown that if (g1,b1)(g_{1},b_{1}) and (g2,b2)(g_{2},b_{2}) are exact Anosov magnetic systems which are smoothly conjugate, then Area​(g1)=Area​(g2)\text{Area}(g_{1})=\text{Area}(g_{2}). In fact, this also extends to (g1,b1+δ)(g_{1},b_{1}+\delta) and (g2,b2+δ)(g_{2},b_{2}+\delta), provided that δ∈ℝ\delta\in\mathds{R} is sufficiently small so that the marked length spectrum still makes sense. With this in mind, the following is immediate.

Corollary 1.5.

Let MM be a closed, connected, orientable surface, and let (g1,b1)(g_{1},b_{1}) and (g2,b2)(g_{2},b_{2}) be exact Anosov magnetic systems on MM. If δ∈ℝ\delta\in\mathds{R} is sufficiently small so that (g1,b1+δ)(g_{1},b_{1}+\delta) and (g2,b2+δ)(g_{2},b_{2}+\delta) are still Anosov and MLS⁡(g1,b1+δ)=MLS⁡(g2,b2+δ){\rm MLS}(g_{1},b_{1}+\delta)={\rm MLS}(g_{2},b_{2}+\delta), then there exists a diffeomorphism f:M→Mf:M\rightarrow M which is isotopic to the identity and which satisfies f∗​(g2)=g1f^{*}(g_{2})=g_{1} and b2∘f=b1b_{2}\circ f=b_{1}.

Notice that there is no assumption on the metric in Corollary  1.5 – as long as the exact magnetic systems (gi,bi+δ)(g_{i},b_{i}+\delta) share the same marked length spectrum, then the underlying metrics are isometric. As previously mentioned, notice that MLS⁡(g,b){\rm MLS}(g,b) encodes the length of the unique closed curve γ\gamma in each non-trivial free homotopy class of MM with prescribed gg-geodesic curvature equal to b∘γb\circ\gamma. The above result can then be interpreted as saying that the unit speed curves with gg-geodesic curvature equal to bb completely determine the underlying metric, provided the set of these curves is “dynamically rich.” In Section  4, we modify the example in [11, Section 7] to construct an example of a metric gg which is not Anosov, but for which there exists an magnetic intensity bb so that [b​Ωg]=0[b\Omega_{g}]=0 and the magnetic system (g,b)(g,b) is Anosov. Thus, Corollary  1.5 along with this example shows that marked length spectrum rigidity can be extended beyond the setting of Anosov metrics and non-positively curved metrics.

Next, we see how the magnetic marked length spectra uniquely characterizes geodesic flows, provided the area is fixed. Using the arguments in [25, Théorème 7.3], one can show that if (g1,b)(g_{1},b) and g2g_{2} both satisfy 𝕂g1,b,Kg2<0\mathbb{K}^{g_{1},b},K^{g_{2}}<0, MLS​(g1,b)=MLS​(g2)\text{MLS}(g_{1},b)=\text{MLS}(g_{2}), and Area​(g1)=Area​(g2)\text{Area}(g_{1})=\text{Area}(g_{2}), then b≡0b\equiv 0 and g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} are isometric. One can also deduce from Lemma 2.2 that if MLS⁡(g1,b)=MLS⁡(g2){\rm MLS}(g_{1},b)={\rm MLS}(g_{2}) and Area​(g1)=Area​(g2)\text{Area}(g_{1})=\text{Area}(g_{2}), then [b​Ωg]=0[b\Omega_{g}]=0. This shows that Corollary  1.5 extends [25, Théorème 7.3] from negatively curved magnetic systems to Anosov magnetic systems.

Corollary 1.6.

Let (g1,b)(g_{1},b) be an Anosov magnetic system. If g2g_{2} is an Anosov metric such that MLS⁡(g1,b)=MLS⁡(g2){\rm MLS}(g_{1},b)={\rm MLS}(g_{2}) and Area⁡(g1)=Area⁡(g2){\rm Area}(g_{1})={\rm Area}(g_{2}), then b≡0b\equiv 0 and there is an isometry between g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} which is isotopic to the identity.

Finally, we introduce the magnetic marked length spectrum rigidity problem in higher dimensions; for more details on this setting, we direct this reader to [4, 5]. Let MM be a closed, connected manifold of arbitrary dimension. A magnetic system is a pair (g,σ)(g,\sigma), where gg is a Riemannian metric and σ\sigma is a closed 22-form (referred to as the magnetic form). Note that the magnetic form generalizes the magnetic intensity bb introduced for surfaces: if σ\sigma is a closed 22-form on a surface, then the magnetic intensity is precisely the unique smooth function bb on MM for which σ=b​Ωg\sigma=b\Omega_{g}. A (g,σ)(g,\sigma)-geodesic is a curve γ:ℝ→M\gamma:\mathds{R}\to M which satisfies the equation

(1.4) D​γ˙d​t​(t)=Y​(γ˙​(t)),\frac{{\rm D}\dot{\gamma}}{{\rm d}t}(t)=Y(\dot{\gamma}(t)),

where Y:T​M→T​MY:TM\to TM is the Lorentz operator defined by the relation g⁡(Y⁡(v),w)=σ⁡(v,w)g(Y(v),w)=\sigma(v,w) for all v,w∈T​M.v,w\in TM. As in the surface case, solutions of (1.4) have constant speed, and the magnetic flow φg,σt:Sg​M→Sg​M\varphi_{g,\sigma}^{t}:S_{g}M\rightarrow S_{g}M associated to (g,σ)(g,\sigma) is the flow on Sg​MS_{g}M induced by (1.4). A pair (g,σ)(g,\sigma) is Anosov if the flow φg,σt\varphi_{g,\sigma}^{t} is Anosov, and as before the magnetic marked length spectrum naturally generalies to Anosov pairs (g,σ)(g,\sigma). With this in mind, a natural question is the following.

Question 1.7.

Let (g1,σ1)(g_{1},\sigma_{1}) and (g2,σ2)(g_{2},\sigma_{2}) be two Anosov magnetic systems on a closed, connected, oriented manifold MM. If MLS⁡(g1,σ1)=MLS⁡(g2,σ2){\rm MLS}(g_{1},\sigma_{1})={\rm MLS}(g_{2},\sigma_{2}), Vol⁡(g1)=Vol⁡(g2)\mathrm{Vol}(g_{1})=\mathrm{Vol}(g_{2}), and [σ1]=[σ2][\sigma_{1}]=[\sigma_{2}], is it true that g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} must be isometric?

As evidence towards a positive answer for this question, suppose that g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} are two Anosov metrics with non-positive sectional curvature. If (g1,σ1)(g_{1},\sigma_{1}) is an Anosov magnetic system satisfying MLS⁡(g1,σ1)=MLS⁡(g2){\rm MLS}(g_{1},\sigma_{1})={\rm MLS}(g_{2}) and Vol​(g1)=Vol​(g2)\text{Vol}(g_{1})=\text{Vol}(g_{2}), then it follows from the fact that geodesics are the unique length minimizers in their free homotopy class that MLS⁡(g1)≤MLS⁡(g2){\rm MLS}(g_{1})\leq{\rm MLS}(g_{2}). As long as the metrics are sufficiently close according to [27, Theorem 2], we have that g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} are isometric and σ1≡0\sigma_{1}\equiv 0.22 2 Note that one can also use this argument along with [15, Theorem 1.1] to deduce Corollary  1.6 in the case where g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} are negatively curved metrics.

2. Preliminaries

Throughout, let MM be a closed, connected, oriented surface, let (g,b)(g,b) be a magnetic system on MM, and let πg:Sg​M→M\pi_{g}:S_{g}M\rightarrow M be the footprint map for the unit tangent bundle. The geodesic vector field XgX^{g} is the infinitesimal generator of the geodesic flow φgt\varphi_{g}^{t} on Sg​MS_{g}M. Since MM is oriented, we may consider the rotation flow ρgt:Sg​M→Sg​M\rho^{t}_{g}:S_{g}M\rightarrow S_{g}M, given by ρgt​(x,v)≔(x,ei​t​v)\rho^{t}_{g}(x,v)\coloneqq(x,e^{it}v). Its infinitesimal generator is the vertical vector field, which we denote by VgV^{g}. Finally, the horizontal vector field on Sg​MS_{g}M is the vector field given by Hg≔[Vg,Xg]H^{g}\coloneqq[V^{g},X^{g}]. Observe that the vector fields Xg,Hg,X^{g},H^{g}, and VgV^{g} form a global frame on Sg​MS_{g}M, which we refer to as Cartan’s moving frame. They satisfy the relations

(2.1) [Vg,Hg]=−Xg,[Vg,Xg]=Hg,[Xg,Hg]=πg∗​(Kg)​Vg,[V^{g},H^{g}]=-X^{g},\quad[V^{g},X^{g}]=H^{g},\quad[X^{g},H^{g}]=\pi_{g}^{*}(K^{g})V^{g},

where KgK^{g} is the Gaussian curvature on MM. Dual to these vector fields are the 11-forms αg,βg,\alpha^{g},\beta^{g}, and ψg\psi^{g} on Sg​MS_{g}M, which we refer to as Cartan’s moving coframe. Using (2.1), one can show that they satisfy the relations

(2.2) d​αg=ψg∧βg,d​βg=−ψg∧αg,d​ψg=−πg∗​(Kg)​αg∧βg.{\mathrm{d}}\alpha^{g}=\psi^{g}\wedge\beta^{g},\quad{\mathrm{d}}\beta^{g}=-\psi^{g}\wedge\alpha^{g},\quad{\mathrm{d}}\psi^{g}=-\pi_{g}^{*}(K^{g})\alpha^{g}\wedge\beta^{g}.

Notice that πg∗​(Ωg)=αg∧βg\pi_{g}^{*}(\Omega_{g})=\alpha^{g}\wedge\beta^{g}, hence we can rewrite the last relation as

(2.3) d​ψg=−πg∗​(Kg​Ωg).{\mathrm{d}}\psi^{g}=-\pi_{g}^{*}(K^{g}\Omega_{g}).

Moreover, the Liouville volume form μg\mu^{g} satisfies μg=αg∧βg∧ψg\mu^{g}=\alpha^{g}\wedge\beta^{g}\wedge\psi^{g}.

Next, observe that the flow φg,bt\varphi_{g,b}^{t} is a Hamiltonian flow, induced by the function H:T​M→ℝH:TM\rightarrow\mathds{R} given by H⁡(x,v)≔12​gx​(v,v)H(x,v)\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}g_{x}(v,v) and the symplectic form given by

(2.4) ωg,b≔−d​αg+πg∗​(b​Ωg).\omega_{g,b}\coloneqq-{\mathrm{d}}\alpha_{g}+\pi_{g}^{*}(b\Omega_{g}).

With this, we now have the tools to prove the following.

Lemma 2.1.

Let (g1,b1)(g_{1},b_{1}) and (g2,b2)(g_{2},b_{2}) be Anosov magnetic systems on MM, smoothly conjugate via h:Sg1​M→Sg2​Mh:S_{g_{1}}M\rightarrow S_{g_{2}}M; then:

h∗​(μg2)=Area⁡(g2)Area⁡(g1)​μg1.\displaystyle h^{*}(\mu^{g_{2}})=\frac{{\rm Area}(g_{2})}{{\rm Area}(g_{1})}\mu^{g_{1}}.
Proof.

±cg2,b2∫γ2b2+∫γ2θ2=−cg1,b1∫γ1b1+∫γ1[θ1+ω].\pm c_{g_{2},b_{2}}\int_{\gamma_{2}}b_{2}+\int_{\gamma_{2}}\theta_{2}=-c_{g_{1},b_{1}}\int_{\gamma_{1}}b_{1}+\int_{\gamma_{1}}[\theta_{1}+\omega].

Another characterization of (g,b)(g,b)-geodesics is that they are minimizers of a functional that behaves like the length functional. More precisely, let (g,b)(g,b) now be an Anosov magnetic system on MM. Inside of every non-trivial free homotopy class ν∈π1​(M)\nu\in\pi_{1}(M) there exists a unique (g,b)(g,b)-geodesic γν∈ν\gamma_{\nu}\in\nu [13]. Given a closed curve γ:S1→M\gamma:S^{1}\rightarrow M in the free homotopy class ν\nu, we define Σg,b​(γ)\Sigma_{g,b}(\gamma) to be a 22-chain on MM with boundary given by γ−γν\gamma-\gamma_{\nu}. With this, we can define the magnetic length of an arbitrary closed curve γ\gamma to be

(2.10) Lg,b​(γ)≔ℓg​(γ)+∫Σg,b​(γ)b​Ωg,L_{g,b}(\gamma)\coloneqq\ell_{g}(\gamma)+\int_{\Sigma_{g,b}(\gamma)}b\Omega_{g},

where ℓg\ell_{g} denotes the (Riemannian) length of the curve with respect to the metric gg. Notice that Lg,bL_{g,b} is well-defined by [36, Lemma 2.2] and, in particular, we have the following.

Lemma 2.4 ([6, 36]).

Let (g,b)(g,b) be an Anosov magnetic system on MM. If γ:S1→M\gamma:S^{1}\rightarrow M is an arbitrary closed curve inside of a free homotopy class ν\nu, then

Lg,b​(γν)≤Lg,b​(γ).L_{g,b}(\gamma_{\nu})\leq L_{g,b}(\gamma).

Finally, it will be convenient to work with an abstract circle bundle which is independent of the choice of metric. Namely, let S​MSM be the principal circle bundle over MM with p:S​M→Mp:SM\rightarrow M is the projection map, and the fibers are given by SxM=(TxM∖{0})/∼S_{x}M=(T_{x}M\smallsetminus\{0\})/\sim, where v∼wv\sim w if and only if v=C​wv=Cw with C>0C>0. Given any Riemannian metric gg on MM, we can identify Sg​MS_{g}M with S​MSM by sending vectors to their equivalence classes. When working on S​MSM, we will use the same symbol to identify all objects from Sg​MS_{g}M identified in S​MSM.

3. Proof of Theorem  1.3

The goal of this section is to prove the following theorem.

Theorem 3.1.

Let MM be a closed, connected, oriented surface, and let ρ∈C∞​(M,ℝ+){\rho\in C^{\infty}(M,\mathds{R}^{+})}. Suppose (g,b1)(g,b_{1}) and (ρ​g,b2)(\rho g,b_{2}) are two Anosov magnetic systems on MM satisfying the following conditions:

MLS⁡(g,b1)=MLS⁡(ρ​g,b2),Area⁡(g)=Area⁡(ρ​g),and​[b1​Ωg]=[b2​Ωg].{\rm MLS}(g,b_{1})={\rm MLS}(\rho g,b_{2}),\ {\rm Area}(g)={\rm Area}(\rho g),\ \mbox{and}\ [b_{1}\Omega_{g}]=[b_{2}\Omega_{g}].

Then ρ≡1\rho\equiv 1 and b1=b2b_{1}=b_{2}.

Observe that [18, Theorem 1.1] reduces Theorem  1.3 to this setting, and thus it is sufficient to work in this conformal setting. The proof that we present below follows, to some extent, the strategy of the proof in  [30, Theorem 2] for Riemanian geodesics. In order to adapt the argument presented there to our setting, we need to compare the magnetic length functional defined above with the Riemannian length functional. This comparison requires the lemma below, which allows us to bound the difference between the two functionals. Let h:S​M→S​Mh:SM\rightarrow SM denote the conjugacy described in the Introduction on the level of S​MSM, and note that if [b1​Ωg1]=[b2​Ωg2][b_{1}\Omega_{g_{1}}]=[b_{2}\Omega_{g_{2}}], then b2​Ωg2−b1​Ωg1=d​ζb_{2}\Omega_{g_{2}}-b_{1}\Omega_{g_{1}}={\mathrm{d}}\zeta for some 11-form ζ\zeta on MM.

Lemma 3.2.

Let MM be a closed, connected, oriented surface. Suppose (g1,b1)(g_{1},b_{1}) and (g2,b2)(g_{2},b_{2}) are two Anosov magnetic systems on MM satisfying the following properties:

Then for every homologically trivial closed (g1,b1)(g_{1},b_{1})-geodesic γ1\gamma_{1}, we have

(3.1) ∫Σg2,b2​(γ1)b2​Ωg2=∫γ1ζ.\int_{\Sigma_{g_{2},b_{2}}(\gamma_{1})}b_{2}\Omega_{g_{2}}=\int_{\gamma_{1}}\zeta.
Proof.

As in (2.8), write b1​Ωg1=cg1,b1​Kg1​Ωg1+d​θ1b_{1}\Omega_{g_{1}}=c_{g_{1},b_{1}}K^{g_{1}}\Omega_{g_{1}}+{\mathrm{d}}\theta_{1}, and define the 11-form κ≔−cg1,b1​ψg1+p∗​(θ1){\kappa\coloneqq-c_{g_{1},b_{1}}\psi^{g_{1}}+p^{*}(\theta_{1})} on S​MSM. ∫Σg2,b2​(γ1)b2​Ωg2=∫Σ~g2,b2​(γ1)p∗​(b2​Ωg2)=[∫γ1κ⁡(Xg1,b1)−∫γ2κ⁡(Xg2,b2)]+[∫γ1ζ−∫γ2ζ],\begin{split}\int_{\Sigma_{g_{2},b_{2}}(\gamma_{1})}b_{2}\Omega_{g_{2}}&=\int_{\tilde{\Sigma}_{g_{2},b_{2}}(\gamma_{1})}p^{*}(b_{2}\Omega_{g_{2}})\\ &=\left[\int_{\gamma_{1}}\kappa(X_{g_{1},b_{1}})-\int_{\gamma_{2}}\kappa(X_{g_{2},b_{2}})\right]+\left[\int_{\gamma_{1}}\zeta-\int_{\gamma_{2}}\zeta\right],\end{split}

where γ2\gamma_{2} is the image of γ1\gamma_{1} by hh, i.e. the (g1,b1)(g_{1},b_{1})-geodesic in the same homotopy class as γ2\gamma_{2}. We can then rewrite this as

Next, using Lemma  2.1 and (2.5), we deduce that h∗​(ωg1,b1)=ωg2,b2h_{*}(\omega_{g_{1},b_{1}})=\omega_{g_{2},b_{2}}. Substituting (3.3) into (3.2), the result follows. ∎

Remark 3.3.

Notice that if we have [b1​Ωg1]=−[b2​Ωg2][b_{1}\Omega_{g_{1}}]=-[b_{2}\Omega_{g_{2}}], so b2​Ωg2+b1​Ωg1=d​ζ{b_{2}\Omega_{g_{2}}+b_{1}\Omega_{g_{1}}={\mathrm{d}}\zeta}, then (3.3) becomes

∫Σg2,b2​(γ1)b2Ωg2=−2∫γ2κ(Xg2,b2)+∫γ1ζ.\int_{\Sigma_{g_{2},b_{2}}(\gamma_{1})}b_{2}\Omega_{g_{2}}=-2\int_{\gamma_{2}}\kappa(X_{g_{2},b_{2}})+\int_{\gamma_{1}}\zeta.

With Lemma  3.2 in hand, we can now prove the result.

The non-positive Livshits theorem [33, Theorem 1] implies that there are Hölder continuous functions F:Sg1​M→[0,∞)F:S_{g_{1}}M\rightarrow[0,\infty) and V:Sg1​M→ℝV:S_{g_{1}}M\rightarrow\mathds{R} such that θ2−θ1−ω=Xg1,b1​(V)+F\theta_{2}-\theta_{1}-\omega=X_{g_{1},b_{1}}(V)+F. Integrating this over Sg1​MS_{g_{1}}M with respect to the normalized Liouville measure, we have

0=∫Sg1​M[θ2−θ1−ω]​d​λg1=∫Sg1​MF​d​λg1.0=\int_{S_{g_{1}}M}[\theta_{2}-\theta_{1}-\omega]{\mathrm{d}}\lambda_{g_{1}}=\int_{S_{g_{1}}M}F{\mathrm{d}}\lambda_{g_{1}}.

Thus, F≡0F\equiv 0. Using [17, Theorem B], we see that θ2−θ1−ω\theta_{2}-\theta_{1}-\omega is an exact 11-form on MM, hence θ2−θ1\theta_{2}-\theta_{1} is closed. Finally, observe that (b2−b1)​Ωg=d⁡(θ2−θ1)=0(b_{2}-b_{1})\Omega_{g}={\mathrm{d}}(\theta_{2}-\theta_{1})=0 by (2.8), hence b2=b1b_{2}=b_{1}. ∎

4. Examples

The goal of this section is to construct a series of examples in order to better understand the assumptions in Theorem  1.3, as well as to understand how Corollary  1.5 compares to known results on marked length spectrum rigidity. As a first step, we show how the area assumption cannot be removed.

Lemma 4.1.

Let MM be a closed, connected, oriented surface, and let gg be a hyperbolic metric on MM. We have MLS(g,b)=(1−b2)−1/2MLS(g){{\rm MLS}(g,b)=(1-b^{2})^{-1/2}{\rm MLS}(g)} for every constant |b|<1|b|<1.

In particular, consider the homothetic metric gb≔(1−b2)−1​gg_{b}\coloneqq(1-b^{2})^{-1}g. Lemma  4.1 shows that MLS⁡(gb)=MLS⁡(g,b){\rm MLS}(g_{b})={\rm MLS}(g,b) and Area​(g)≠Area​(gb)\text{Area}(g)\neq\text{Area}(g_{b}), and thus the area assumption in Theorem  1.3 is necessary.

Proof of Lemma  4.1.

We lift the magnetic system to the universal cover ℍ={(x,y)∈ℝ2,y>0}\mathbb{H}=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2},\ y>0\}. Denote the lifted magnetic system on ℍ\mathbb{H} by (g~,b)(\tilde{g},b), where g~\tilde{g} is given by g~=y−1​(d​x2+d​y2)\tilde{g}=y^{-1}({\mathrm{d}}x^{2}+{\mathrm{d}}y^{2}). In particular, MM can viewed as the quotient of ℍ\mathbb{H} under the action of a cocompact lattice Γ\Gamma in PSL​(2,ℝ)\text{PSL}(2,\mathds{R}).

Let ν∈π1​(M)\nu\in\pi_{1}(M), and let γ:ℝ→M\gamma:\mathds{R}\to M the unique closed gg-geodesic representative. Without loss of generality we can assume that the lifted geodesic γ~\tilde{\gamma} is of the form γ~​(ℝ)={(0,r)∈ℝ2|r>0}\tilde{\gamma}(\mathds{R})=\{(0,r)\in\mathds{R}^{2}\ |\ r>0\}. In particular, there exists an isometry f∈Γf\in\Gamma so that f​(γ~​(t))=γ~​(t+ℓ)f(\tilde{\gamma}(t))=\tilde{\gamma}(t+\ell) for every t∈ℝt\in\mathds{R} (see, for example, [19]). Since ff fixes (0,1)(0,1) and the point at infinity, we deduce that f⁡(x,y)=eℓg​(γ)​(x,y)f(x,y)=e^{\ell_{g}(\gamma)}(x,y), thus

ℓg​(γ)=∫1eℓg​(γ)d​yy.\ell_{g}(\gamma)=\int_{1}^{e^{\ell_{g}(\gamma)}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{y}.

Let γb:ℝ→M\gamma_{b}:\mathds{R}\to M be the unique closed (g,b)(g,b)-geodesic with free homotopy class ν\nu. Notice that we have γ~b​(ℝ)={(r​b,r⁡(1−b2))|r>0}\tilde{\gamma}_{b}(\mathds{R})=\{\left(rb,r(1-b^{2})\right)\ |\ r>0\} and f⁡(b,1−b2)=(eℓg​(γ)​b,eℓg​(γ)​(1−b2)){f(b,1-b^{2})=\left(e^{\ell_{g}(\gamma)}b,e^{\ell_{g}(\gamma)}(1-b^{2})\right)}, hence

ℓg​(γb)=∫1eℓg​(γ)d​yy​1−b2=ℓg​(γ)1−b2.\ell_{g}(\gamma_{b})=\int_{1}^{e^{\ell_{g}(\gamma)}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{y\sqrt{1-b^{2}}}=\frac{\ell_{g}(\gamma)}{\sqrt{1-b^{2}}}.

The result follows. ∎

Next, we show how the assumption on the cohomology classes in Theorem  1.3 cannot be removed.

Lemma 4.2.

Let MM be a closed, connected, oriented surface, and let gg be a hyperbolic metric on MM. We have MLS⁡(g,b)=MLS⁡(g,−b){{\rm MLS}(g,b)={\rm MLS}(g,-b)} for every constant |b|<1|b|<1.

Proof of Lemma  4.2.

Define

Xg,b≔12​(1b−b−1).X^{g,b}\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1&b\\ -b&-1\end{pmatrix}.

It is well-known that there is a cocompact lattice Γ\Gamma in PSL​(2,ℝ)\text{PSL}(2,\mathds{R}) such that the magnetic flow associated to (g,b)(g,b) on Sg​MS_{g}M can be interpreted as the flow on Γ\PSL​(2,ℝ)\Gamma\backslash\text{PSL}(2,\mathds{R}) given by φtg,b​(Γ​q)≔Γ​q​et​Xb\varphi^{g,b}_{t}(\Gamma q)\coloneqq\Gamma qe^{tX^{b}} (see, for example, [39]). Observe that the matrix c∈SL​(2,ℝ)c\in\text{SL}(2,\mathds{R}) given by

c≔11−b2​(1−b−b1)c\coloneqq\frac{1}{1-b^{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&-b\\ -b&1\end{pmatrix}

satisfies the condition that Xg,b​c=c​Xg,−bX^{g,b}c=cX^{g,-b}. Thus, an easy argument using induction and the definition of the exponential map tells us that if we define the map h:Γ\PSL​(2,ℝ)→Γ\PSL​(2,ℝ)h:\Gamma\backslash\text{PSL}(2,\mathds{R})\rightarrow\Gamma\backslash\text{PSL}(2,\mathds{R}) by h⁡(Γ​q)≔Γ​q​c,h(\Gamma q)\coloneqq\Gamma qc, then we have h∘φg,bt=φg,−bt∘hh\circ\varphi_{g,b}^{t}=\varphi_{g,-b}^{t}\circ h. This is a smooth conjugacy between the magnetic flows for (g,b)(g,b) and (g,−b)(g,-b). Furthermore, if we define a family of matrices cs∈SL​(2,ℝ)c_{s}\in\text{SL}(2,\mathds{R}) by

cs≔11−s​b2​(1−s​b−s​b1),c_{s}\coloneqq\frac{1}{1-sb^{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&-sb\\ -sb&1\end{pmatrix},

then we have an associated family of maps hs:Γ\PSL​(2,ℝ)→Γ\PSL​(2,ℝ)h_{s}:\Gamma\backslash\text{PSL}(2,\mathds{R})\rightarrow\Gamma\backslash\text{PSL}(2,\mathds{R}) given by hs​(Γ​q)≔Γ​q​csh_{s}(\Gamma q)\coloneqq\Gamma qc_{s}. Observe that the family is continuous in ss and satisfies h0=Idh_{0}=\text{Id} and h1=hh_{1}=h, so hh is homotopic to the identity. As discussed in [10, Section 10.3] and [14, Section 3], the subgroup of π1​(S​M)\pi_{1}(SM) generated by the kernel of the footprint map equals the center of π1​(S​M)\pi_{1}(SM). Since hh is invertible, we have that h∗h_{*} is an isomorphism on the level of the fundamental groups, hence induces an isomorphism on the level of π1​(M)\pi_{1}(M). This shows that MLS⁡(g,b)=MLS⁡(g,−b){\rm MLS}(g,b)={\rm MLS}(g,-b). ∎

Finally, we construct an example of a closed, oriented, connected surface such that there exists an exact Anosov magnetic system (g,b)(g,b) where the metric gg is not Anosov by modifying the arguments in [11, Section 7]. This shows that it is not necessary to assume that gg is Anosov in Corollary  1.5. We recall the following lemma, and briefly sketch its proof. For more details, we point the reader to [11, Sections 6 and 7].

Lemma 4.3.

There exists a closed, connected, orientable surface MM and an Anosov magnetic system (g,b)(g,b) on MM with bb constant such that gg is not Anosov.

Sketch of Proof.

We will need the following.

Lemma 4.4 ([11, Lemma 6.1]).

Let (g,b)(g,b) be a magnetic system on MM. If there are constants T>0T>0 and H>1H>1 such that for any (g,b)(g,b)-geodesic γ\gamma and any solution uu to the magnetic Riccati equation

has gug_{u}-geodesic curvature kgu​(t)=±u⁡(s)\mathrm{k}^{g_{u}}(t)=\pm u(s). In particular, αs±\alpha_{s}^{\pm} is a closed gug_{u}-geodesic if and only if u⁡(s)=0u(s)=0 [11, Lemma 6.2]. For δ>0\delta>0 small, consider the interval [−δ,δ]⊂[−1/4,1/4][-\delta,\delta]\subset[-1/4,1/4]. Let u⁡(s)=tanh⁡(s)u(s)=\mathrm{tanh}(s), except for a small C0C^{0} perturbation in the interval [−δ,δ][-\delta,\delta] where the function uu satisfies the following:

  • •

The goal is to now modify this argument in order to derive the following.

Lemma 4.5.

There exists a closed, connected, orientable surface MM and an exact Anosov magnetic system (g,b)(g,b) on MM such that gg is not Anosov.

We briefly sketch the idea of the proof. The first step is to modify Lemma  4.3 in order to allow a magnetic intensity b+b_{+} which is a small positive bump function. In particular, this will show that any (g,b+)(g,b_{+})-geodesic must spend a small amount of time in the “bad region,” and we can shrink this amount of time as necessary. A symmetric argument will also show that one can use the magnetic intensity b−=−b+b_{-}=-b_{+}, and any (g,b−)(g,b_{-}) geodesic will also spend the same amount of time in the “bad region.” By gluing together these examples and taking the magnetic intensity b≔b++b−b\coloneqq b_{+}+b_{-} (note that these are supported on two disjoint regions), we see that any magnetic geodesic can only spend a small amount of time in the “bad regions,” and adjusting parameters can shrink this amount of time to be arbitrarily small. As long as we take TT sufficiently large depending on the distance between the “bad regions,” as well as their size, then we can find an HH where Lemma  4.4 applies. Moreover, since these “bad regions,” have the same size, we see that the average of bb with respect to the area is zero, and hence this gives an example of an exact Anosov magnetic system whose underlying metric is not Anosov. We now present the details.

Proof of Lemma  4.5.

We use the same notation as in the sketch of Lemma  4.3. The goal is to construct a magnetic intensity which is compactly supported on NN, and whose growth is small. This will allow us to control the magnetic curvature as in the previous argument. Fix ϵ>0\epsilon>0 sufficiently small, and let δ2>δ1≫1/4\delta_{2}>\delta_{1}\gg 1/4. Let vv be a C0C^{0} perturbation of uu such that vv coincides with uu on the interval [−δ1,δ1][-\delta_{1},\delta_{1}], Kgv​(s)≤1K^{g_{v}}(s)\leq 1 for |δ1|≤|s|≤|δ2||\delta_{1}|\leq|s|\leq|\delta_{2}| and Kgv​(s)=−1−ϵK^{g_{v}}(s)=-1-\epsilon for |s|>δ2|s|>\delta_{2}.

Let δ4≫δ3≫δ2\delta_{4}\gg\delta_{3}\gg\delta_{2}. Let b+b_{+} be a bump function with the following properties:

  • •

    b+b_{+} is supported in [−δ4,δ4][-\delta_{4},\delta_{4}]

  • •

    0≤b+≤1/20\leq b_{+}\leq 1/2 and b+≡1/2b_{+}\equiv 1/2 on [−δ2,δ2][-\delta_{2},\delta_{2}],

  • •

    ‖d​b+‖∞+b+2<1/4+ϵ\|\mathrm{d}b_{+}\|_{\infty}+b_{+}^{2}<1/4+\epsilon.

The magnetic curvature associated to (gv,b+)(g_{v},b_{+}) satisfies the property that Kg,b+​(s)=Kg,1/2≤1/2K^{g,b_{+}}(s)=K^{g,1/2}\leq 1/2 for s∈[−δ,δ]s\in[-\delta,\delta], and Kg,b+(s)≤−3/4K^{g,b_{+}}(s)\leq-3/4 otherwise. By construction, the dynamics of (gv,b+)(g_{v},b_{+}) restricted on C1/4C_{1/4} coincides with the dynamics of (g,1/2)(g,1/2). Involving the same argument as in Lemma  4.3, we can conclude that the time any (gv,b+)(g_{v},b_{+})-geodesic spends in CδC_{\delta} is bounded above by 2​tδ2t_{\delta} for a constant tδ>0t_{\delta}>0 depending on the parameters. Let b−≔−b+b_{-}\coloneqq-b_{+}. By symmetry, the time any (gv,b−)(g_{v},b_{-})-geodesic spends in CδC_{\delta} is bounded above by 2​tδ2t_{\delta} for the same constant tδ>0t_{\delta}>0. For both of these examples, preform the same compactification procedure to get a closed, connected, oriented surface, and two magnetic systems (g¯v,b±)(\bar{g}_{v},b_{\pm}).

Away from the neighborhoods CδC_{\delta}, we take two open sets and glue together two copies of (M,g¯v)(M,\bar{g}_{v}) along these open sets to get M¯=[M∪M]gv\bar{M}=\left[M\cup M\right]_{g_{v}}. Equip this new surface M¯\bar{M} with the magnetic system (g¯v,b)(\bar{g}_{v},b), where b≔b++b−b\coloneqq b_{+}+b_{-}. By construction, the time each unit speed (g,b)(g,b)-geodesic connected segment spends in the region corresponding through the glue to CδC_{\delta} is still bounded by tδt_{\delta}. Outside those regions, the magnetic curvature is negative and still bounded by −3/4-3/4, and thus by taking TT sufficiently large depending on the distance between the regions CδC_{\delta}, and taking HH depending on tδt_{\delta} and this distance, one can conclude from Lemma  4.4 that the corresponding flow is Anosov. Moreover, we have

∫M¯b​Ωg=2​π​[∫−δ4δ4b+​𝑑s+∫−δ4δ4b−​𝑑s]=0,\int_{\bar{M}}b\Omega_{g}=2\pi\left[\int_{-\delta_{4}}^{\delta_{4}}b_{+}\mathrm{d}s+\int_{-\delta_{4}}^{\delta_{4}}b_{-}\mathrm{d}s\right]=0,

hence the system is exact. ∎
